title: No "I have attained" (section 9)
hook: a stream-enterer does not think "I have entered the stream"; Subhuti rests in peace without that thought
tomorrow: A mind that rests on nothing (section 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, four lines: even a short verse, kept and passed on, outweighs worlds of treasure. Your line: four lines. Who got your four lines? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

At some dinner parties there's a guest who mentions, more than once, how little he cares about status. The more he says it, the less it sounds true. Section nine of the Diamond Sutra is about the quiet opposite of that guest. The Buddha walks Subhuti down the stages of the path, one at a time, and at every step he asks the same thing. Does someone who has reached this stage think, I have reached it? Then, at the end, Subhuti answers for himself, and he's the one the Buddha has praised. Today: no "I have attained."
screen: `THE GUEST WHO SAYS HE'S HUMBLE.` → `THE SAME QUESTION AT EVERY STEP.` → `SUBHUTI ANSWERS FOR HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the stages. Early Buddhist teaching names the stages of the path: the stream-enterer, who has entered the current that leads to awakening; the once-returner; the non-returner; and the arhat, the worthy one, fully freed. Second, the question at the first stage. Does a stream-enterer think, I have entered the stream? No, Subhuti says. And the reason is the sutra's own kind of reason. A stream-enterer enters nothing. Not sights, not sounds, not smells, tastes, touches or things of the mind. That's exactly why the name stream-enterer can be used. The Buddha asks the same question at each stage, and the answer comes back the same each time. An arhat who thought, I am an arhat, would be holding on to a self, a person, a being, a life, the very things the path lets go of. Third, Subhuti on himself. The Buddha has praised him, he says, as one who dwells in peace, free of craving. But I don't think, I am an arhat free of craving. If I thought that, the Buddha wouldn't have said that Subhuti delights in peaceful dwelling. The peace and the thought can't sit in the same chair. Fourth, the credit line. The sutra isn't against reaching anything, or against doing good. It names every stage. What it drops is the credit line that gets written afterward, the small voice that says, look what I did. You carried a neighbor's groceries. Then, a minute later, the narrator arrives to sign it. The groceries were carried either way. Subhuti's peace, the sutra says, has no signature on it.
screen: `THE STAGES OF THE PATH.` · `NO STREAM WAS ENTERED.` · `SUBHUTI DOESN'T SAY IT EITHER.` · `GOOD, WITHOUT THE CREDIT LINE.` · then, large: `NO "I HAVE ATTAINED."`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: do good without the thought, I did. Settle, and breathe. Start with this sit itself. Before long, a little narrator may show up: I'm doing well at this. I'm calmer than yesterday. If it does, don't scold it. Just say it again with the I taken out. Sitting. Breathing. Calm, for now. Then, near the end, name one small thing you'll do for someone after the bell, in the same plain way: door held, call returned, dish washed. Let even those words fade, and stay with the breath. The good can be done without a name on it. The bell holds the time.
No "I have attained." The one who has entered the stream doesn't think, I have entered it; Subhuti dwells in peace without that thought. Today's word.
Your line: without "I did." Today, when you finish a task, sum it up to yourself in two plain words with no I in them: dishes done, call made. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, people are encouraged to do good quietly and to dedicate the merit to others rather than claim it; teachers use this section to warn against pride in one's own progress.

fork.setup: you're Subhuti. the Buddha has praised you for dwelling in peace. he asks whether you think, 'I am an arhat, free of craving.' what do you say?
options: yes: the Buddha said so himself.
no: if I thought that, he couldn't have praised me.
I'm not sure yet; ask me again later.
fork.reveal: Subhuti says he doesn't think it. if he did, the Buddha wouldn't have said Subhuti delights in peaceful dwelling.

original.note: Sanskrit: one who has entered the stream; in Pali, sotapanna.

trapdoor: what you thought: real masters don't reach anything.
what it means: the stages are real, but one who reaches them doesn't hold the thought 'I have reached it.'
what a scholar hears: the sutra runs the early stages of the path, stream-enterer to arhat, through its own logic, so the thought of attaining is the last thing to let go.

notes: Section numbering follows the common 32-section division of Kumarajiva's Chinese text.
All wording paraphrased (quoted: null). The sutra has the Buddha praise Subhuti as foremost among those dwelling in peace (arana); the voice says only 'praised him' to avoid an unneeded superlative.
Stage glosses (stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arhat) are standard; the claims rule was applied by not stating their number.
